title: Handpieces, burs & rotary instruments
blurb: High-speed air turbines and slow-speed handpieces, which bur fits which handpiece, why water coolant matters, and how to look after handpieces.
question: The dentist is about to cut through enamel on a lower molar and then remove soft decay near the pulp. They ask you to load the high-speed with a diamond and the slow-speed with a round steel bur. One bur has a short smooth shank and the other has a notch at the end. Which goes where, and why does the high-speed need water spray?

teach.body: Rotary instruments are burs and polishers spun by a handpiece. The high-speed air turbine is driven by compressed air and spins extremely fast with little torque. It cuts enamel, old restorations and crown preparations quickly. The slow-speed handpiece, driven by an electric or air motor, turns much more slowly with far more torque. It is used for removing soft caries, polishing, finishing and adjusting. Each handpiece only takes burs with a matching shank, so loading the right bur is part of your job.

teach.caption: Air turbines are often quoted as reaching several hundred thousand revolutions per minute. Electric speed-increasing handpieces also take FG burs.

teach.note: Common shapes: round (caries removal and access), pear and fissure (cavity outlines), inverted cone (undercuts), flame (finishing). Diamond burs have a colour band showing grit: green coarse, blue medium, red fine, yellow extra fine.

teach.body: Cutting at high speed creates friction and heat. Without water, the temperature rise can damage the pulp, and the bur clogs and cuts poorly. Water spray cools the tooth and bur and washes debris away. It also creates a spray and aerosol, so you keep the high-volume aspirator close to the tooth being cut, retract the cheek or tongue, and use the 3-in-1 to keep the mirror clear. Check the spray is working before the dentist starts.

teach.caption: Item 2 is a contra-angle handpiece with a bur fitted. Its angled head lets the dentist reach posterior teeth.

teach.h: Looking after a handpiece after each patient

steps.label: Flush
steps.sub: Run water 20–30 s with the bur in

steps.label: Clean
steps.sub: Washer-disinfector or method the maker approves

steps.label: Lubricate
steps.sub: Maker's oil; separate can for cleaned items

teach.caption: Don't put handpieces in an ultrasonic bath unless the manufacturer confirms it is safe. Poor lubrication damages the bearings.

teach.text: An FG bur will NOT lock into a latch (RA) contra-angle, and an RA bur won't grip in a turbine. Never fit or remove a bur while the handpiece is running, and always push the bur fully home: a loose bur can fly out or wobble.

items: Air turbine: compressed air, very fast, low torque, FG burs, water spray essential.
Slow-speed: motor-driven, high torque, RA burs in a contra-angle or HP burs in a straight handpiece.
Ring colours: red speeds up (FG), blue 1:1 (RA), green slows down.
Water coolant protects the pulp; the nurse aspirates close to the tooth.
Flush, remove the bur, clean, lubricate and sterilise to the manufacturer's instructions.

summary: You can now tell a high-speed turbine from a slow-speed handpiece, match FG, RA and HP burs to the right handpiece, read handpiece ring colours, choose bur materials, explain why water coolant protects the pulp, and care for handpieces between patients.

A.q: The dentist asks you to load a bur into the air turbine. Which type of shank must it have?
A.why: Air turbines hold burs by friction in the chuck, so they take short, smooth friction-grip (FG) burs.

whyNot.0: Latch burs have a notch that locks into a slow-speed contra-angle.
whyNot.1: Long HP burs fit the straight handpiece.
whyNot.3: Mandrels carry discs and are used in the slow-speed handpiece.

A.q: Why is water spray essential when the air turbine is cutting tooth tissue?
options: It makes the bur spin faster
It cools the tooth and protects the pulp
It numbs the tooth during cutting
It lubricates the turbine bearings as it runs
A.why: High-speed cutting generates heat. Water spray cools the tooth and bur so the pulp isn't damaged, and washes away debris.

whyNot.0: Speed comes from the compressed air drive, not the water.
whyNot.2: Local anaesthetic numbs the tooth; water has no anaesthetic effect.
whyNot.3: Bearings are lubricated with the manufacturer's oil during reprocessing.

A.q: A slow-speed handpiece has a green ring. What does this tell you?
A.why: Green means speed-reducing: the bur turns slower than the motor with more torque, as used for endodontics or implants.

whyNot.0: Speed-increasing handpieces have a red ring.
whyNot.1: A 1:1 handpiece has a blue ring.
whyNot.2: FG burs are used in red-ring and turbine handpieces.

B.q: Which bur would you choose for the slow-speed contra-angle to remove soft caries?
options: Round bur with a latch shank
Diamond bur with an FG shank
Fissure bur with an HP shank
Flame bur with an FG shank
B.why: Soft caries is usually removed with a round bur at slow speed, and a contra-angle takes latch-type (RA) burs.

whyNot.1: FG diamonds are for the high-speed and cutting enamel.
whyNot.2: HP burs only fit the straight handpiece.
whyNot.3: FG burs won't lock into a latch contra-angle, and flames are for finishing.

B.q: What is the straight handpiece with long HP burs most often used for?
B.why: The straight handpiece with HP burs or acrylic trimmers is used to adjust dentures, and with irrigation in oral surgery.

whyNot.0: Crown preparations are cut with the high-speed and FG diamonds.
whyNot.1: Composite is usually finished with a contra-angle or high-speed finishing bur.
whyNot.3: Old amalgam is removed with the high-speed and plenty of water and suction.

B.q: Which is the correct way to care for a handpiece between patients?
options: Wipe it down, then put it straight back on the hose
Flush it, remove the bur, clean, lubricate, sterilise
Soak it overnight in disinfectant, then wipe dry
Put it through the ultrasonic bath, then sterilise it
B.why: Handpieces are flushed, the bur removed, cleaned by a compatible method, lubricated and sterilised following the manufacturer's instructions.

whyNot.0: Wiping alone leaves internal contamination; handpieces must be reprocessed.
whyNot.2: Soaking can damage handpieces and doesn't sterilise them.
whyNot.3: Ultrasonic baths can damage handpieces unless the manufacturer says otherwise.

C.q: A bur with a small notch at the end of its shank fits which handpiece?
C.why: The notch is the latch that locks into a slow-speed (RA) contra-angle head.

whyNot.0: Air turbines take smooth friction-grip burs.
whyNot.1: Straight handpieces take long, smooth HP burs.
whyNot.2: Red-ring handpieces take FG burs, like a turbine.

C.q: Which bur material is coated with abrasive particles and used mainly in the high-speed?
C.why: Diamond burs have abrasive diamond particles bonded to them and grind enamel efficiently at high speed with water.

whyNot.1: Stainless steel burs are used at slow speed for soft caries.
whyNot.2: Tungsten carbide burs have cutting blades (flutes), not an abrasive coating.
whyNot.3: Carbon steel burs are bladed and blunt quickly; they aren't abrasive-coated.

C.q: A handpiece is becoming noisy and the bur is slipping in the chuck. What is the most likely cause?
options: The water spray is set too high
The bur is the wrong colour band
The aspirator is too close to it
C.why: Inadequate lubrication damages the bearings and chuck, causing noise, vibration and poor bur grip. It should be taken out of use and serviced.

whyNot.0: Water spray volume doesn't affect how the chuck grips the bur.
whyNot.1: The colour band shows grit coarseness, not fit.
whyNot.3: Suction position affects the field, not the handpiece mechanism.

reteach.title: Think of a power drill and a screwdriver
reteach.question: Why would a builder use a fast drill for some jobs and a slow, powerful screwdriver for others?

blocks.h: Fast and light vs slow and strong
blocks.body: The air turbine is like a very fast, lightweight drill: brilliant for cutting hard material quickly, but it stalls if pushed hard, and it gets hot, so it needs water to cool it. The slow-speed is like a powerful screwdriver: it turns slowly but with lots of force, so it suits careful jobs like scooping out soft decay and polishing. Just as a drill bit and a screwdriver bit have different ends, each handpiece only takes burs with the matching shank.

blocks.h: Pick the handpiece, then the bur

explain.body: The air turbine runs on compressed air at very high speed with low torque, so it cuts enamel fast and needs water spray. The slow-speed runs on a motor at lower speed with high torque, for soft caries, polishing and finishing.

test.q: Which handpiece would the dentist normally use to cut through enamel for a crown preparation?
test.why: The air turbine's very high speed, with a diamond FG bur and water spray, cuts enamel quickly and efficiently.

whyNot.0: The straight handpiece is for dentures and surgical bone removal.
whyNot.2: A green-ring handpiece is slow and high-torque, used for endodontics or implants.
whyNot.3: A blue-ring handpiece runs at motor speed, used for caries removal and polishing.

explain.body: FG burs are short and smooth (1.6 mm) and fit the turbine or a red-ring handpiece. RA burs have a latch notch (2.35 mm) and fit the slow-speed contra-angle. HP burs are long and smooth (2.35 mm) and fit the straight handpiece.

test.q: Which bur shank fits a straight handpiece?
test.why: The straight handpiece takes long HP (handpiece) burs.

whyNot.0: FG burs fit air turbines and speed-increasing handpieces.
whyNot.1: RA latch burs fit the slow-speed contra-angle.
whyNot.3: Each handpiece only grips its matching shank type.

explain.body: Heat from high-speed cutting can damage the pulp. Water spray cools the tooth and bur and clears debris. The nurse keeps the high-volume aspirator near the tooth being cut to remove water, debris and aerosol, and keeps the mirror clear.

explain.caption: The deeper the cavity, the closer the bur is to the pulp, and the more cooling matters.

test.q: While the dentist cuts with the air turbine, where should the high-volume aspirator tip be?
options: Close to the tooth being cut
Under the tongue on the far side
Outside the mouth near the lips
test.why: Placing the tip close to the working tooth captures the water spray, debris and aerosol at source.

whyNot.1: The soft palate would trigger the gag reflex.
whyNot.2: Far from the tooth, most of the spray escapes as aerosol.
whyNot.3: Outside the mouth it can't remove fluid or debris effectively.

explain.body: Flush waterlines for 20–30 seconds between patients. Remove the bur, clean the handpiece by a method the manufacturer approves, lubricate it with a separate can of oil kept for cleaned items, and sterilise. Handpieces that aren't oiled properly become noisy, overheat and lose their grip on burs.

test.q: HTM 01-05 says dental unit waterlines should be flushed between patients for at least how long?
test.why: HTM 01-05 advises flushing for at least 20–30 seconds between patients, and at least 2 minutes at the start and end of the day.

whyNot.0: 5 seconds is too short to flush the line.
whyNot.1: 2 minutes is the flush at the start and end of the day.
